youtube.baslik: Room Acoustics: Reverberation and Signal-to-Noise | Lesson 44 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How does the acoustics of a room affect understanding speech? In this lesson we look at direct sound and reflections, reverberation time (RT60), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), critical distance and classroom acoustics targets (35 dBA, 0.6 seconds, SNR of at least +15 dB). We also compare approaches that improve the room and the signal.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: ANSI/ASA S12.60, Acoustical Performance Criteria, Design Requirements, and Guidelines for Schools; ASHA, Guidelines for Addressing Acoustics in Educational Settings (2005); World Health Organization, Guidelines for Community Noise (1999); Crandell CC and Smaldino JJ, Classroom acoustics for children with normal hearing and with hearing impairment (Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools, 2000); ISO 3382, Measurement of room acoustic parameters.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Reverberation time, signal-to-noise ratio, critical distance
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how rooms affect understanding speech, through reverberation and the signal-to-noise ratio.
We will also look at critical distance and the acoustic targets recommended for classrooms.
In a closed room, a talker's voice first reaches the listener directly, along the shortest path.
The sound also strikes the walls, ceiling and floor, and the reflected sounds reach the listener a little later.
Early reflections arriving within about the first fifty milliseconds merge with the direct sound and can strengthen speech.
The cloud of later, gradually decaying reflections is called reverberation.
Reverberation smears speech sounds over one another and reduces intelligibility.

maddeler.metin: Time for a _60 dB_ drop after offset

cumleler.yazi: Reverberation time, or RT60, is the time it takes for the sound level to fall by sixty decibels after the source stops.
cumleler.ses: Reverberation time, or R.T. sixty, is the time it takes for the sound level to fall by sixty decibels after the source stops.

cumleler: A sixty decibel drop means the sound intensity falls to one millionth.

cumleler.yazi: According to the Sabine formula, reverberation time rises with room volume and falls with the total sound absorption of the surfaces.

cumleler: Hard surfaces such as concrete, glass and tiles lengthen it; acoustic ceilings, carpets and curtains absorb sound and shorten it.
It can be measured with the interrupted noise method or by recording the decay of an impulse; both are defined in standards.
Reverberation times differ greatly between environments.
In an acoustically treated classroom, the time is kept at around half a second.
In untreated classrooms with hard surfaces, it can often exceed one second.
Concert halls aim for about two seconds so that music sounds full.
In large places of worship it can rise to several seconds, which makes speech hard to understand.
So a room that is good for music can be poor for understanding speech.
To see the effect of reverberation, think of a word: a strong vowel lingers in the room for a while after it ends.
This tail falls on top of the weak consonant that follows and masks it.
As we saw on the speech banana, vowels are strong and consonants weak, so consonants are lost the most.
As a result, syllable boundaries and word endings become blurred.
When noise and reverberation occur together, they can cause a much greater loss than either one alone.

cumleler.yazi: The signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, is the difference between the level of the target sound and the level of the background noise.

cumleler: For example, if the teacher's voice is sixty five decibels at the ear and the noise is fifty five, the SNR is plus ten decibels.
If the noise is louder than the speech, the SNR is negative.
Because decibels are logarithmic, the difference between two levels actually expresses the ratio of two intensities, hence the name.
Measurements show that the SNR in classrooms often falls below the level recommended for learning.
An adult with normal hearing usually understands speech comfortably at a positive SNR.
That is because language knowledge and context let them easily fill in missing sounds.
Children are still learning language, so they cannot fill in missing sounds; they need a better SNR for the same performance.
People with hearing loss also often need a clearly higher SNR for the same performance.
Older adults, people learning a new language, and children with attention or language difficulties are also more affected by noise.
That is why an SNR of at least plus fifteen decibels at the ear is recommended for children in the classroom.

maddeler.metin: Only _one or two_ meters in classrooms

cumleler: In open space, doubling the distance from the source lowers the direct sound by about six decibels; this is the inverse square law.
In a closed room, however, the reverberant sound is at roughly the same level everywhere in the room.
Close to the source the direct sound dominates; moving away, the direct sound weakens while the reverberant sound stays the same.
The distance at which the direct and reverberant sound levels are equal is called the critical distance.
Beyond the critical distance, the listener hears mainly reverberant sound, and speech clarity drops markedly.
Critical distance grows as the room gets larger and reverberation decreases; in a typical classroom it is only a few meters.
Acoustic targets have been defined so that speech is well understood in classrooms.

cumleler.yazi: The American standard ANSI S12.60 limits noise to 35 dBA and reverberation time to 0.6 seconds for an empty, mid-sized classroom.
cumleler.ses: The American classroom acoustics standard limits noise to thirty five decibels A and reverberation time to zero point six seconds for an empty, mid-sized classroom.

cumleler.yazi: For larger classrooms the reverberation limit is 0.7 seconds.
cumleler.ses: For larger classrooms the reverberation limit is zero point seven seconds.

cumleler.yazi: The World Health Organization also recommends classroom noise not above 35 dBA and a reverberation time of about 0.6 seconds.
cumleler.ses: The World Health Organization also recommends classroom noise not above thirty five decibels A and a reverberation time of about zero point six seconds.

cumleler: The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, or ASHA, adds an SNR of at least plus fifteen decibels at the child's ear.
Other countries have similar guidelines; in Türkiye, too, there is a regulation on protecting buildings against noise.
However, a large share of real classrooms are reported to fall short of these targets.
There are two complementary approaches to improving a classroom; the first is treating the room itself.
Acoustic ceilings, carpets and curtains shorten the reverberation time.
Controlling windows, ventilation and corridor noise lowers background noise.
Treating the room benefits every student in the class.
The second approach is improving the signal.
Remote microphone systems, which send the teacher's voice from a worn microphone straight to the student's device, clearly improve the SNR.
Sound-field systems, which spread the voice evenly through loudspeakers placed in the room, can also be used.
Sitting where the student can see the teacher's face, within the critical distance, is also a simple but effective measure.
These approaches should be considered together, not as substitutes for one another.
Test rooms used for audiometry are also specially designed for low background noise and a short reverberation time.
Directional microphones in hearing aids can improve the SNR somewhat by emphasising speech from the front.
But because reverberant sound arrives from all directions, devices cannot fully remove the effect of reverberation.
In counselling, simple strategies are explained, such as sitting away from the noise source and where the talker's face is visible.

sahneler.metin: When a patient struggles in noise, ask about the setting: room, surfaces, distance, noise source. Halving the distance to the talker raises direct sound by about 6 dB.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: when a patient reports difficulty understanding in noise, ask in detail about the settings where they struggle.
The size of the room, the hardness of the surfaces, the distance to the talker and where the noise comes from all give useful clues.
Halving the distance to the talker raises the direct sound by about six decibels and improves the SNR within the critical distance.
These simple changes can make a clear difference in daily life, independent of device settings.
Reverberation time is the time it takes for the level to fall by sixty decibels after the sound stops.
The signal-to-noise ratio is the difference between speech and noise levels; children and people with hearing loss need a better ratio.
Beyond the critical distance, reverberant sound becomes dominant and speech clarity drops.

cumleler.yazi: For classrooms, the targets are 35 dBA background noise, a 0.6 second reverberation time, and an SNR of at least plus fifteen decibels.
cumleler.ses: For classrooms, the targets are thirty five decibels A background noise, a zero point six second reverberation time, and an SNR of at least plus fifteen decibels.

sahneler.soru: What is the reverberation time target for an empty, mid-sized classroom?
sahneler.aciklama: ANSI S12.60 and ASHA recommend _0.6 seconds_ and 35 dBA background noise for classrooms.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what is the reverberation time target for an empty, mid-sized classroom?
The correct answer is B: 0.6 seconds.
cumleler.ses: The correct answer is B: zero point six seconds.

cumleler: Longer reverberation lets the tails of vowels mask consonants and blurs speech.
